items.title: Delfeayo Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I learned a lot from Ray about the way that he would deliver his music night after night... The hip thing about it, though, is that he went into a blues. He started playing that one note... Ray looks back, and he’s like, “It’s too loud, too loud, damn it, this right here.”

ctx.x: Let me see. You’re 20 years old. You had your first professional gig.

The arrogance of youth. But I learned a lot from the people in the band. They stuck together, and the community, teamwork that was involved. That was my first time in being involved in something other than a sports team that had that many components, had that many people involved. I learned a lot from Ray about the way that he would deliver his music night after night. The one experience that taught me the most – the situations on the road were really kind of – they were not very good. It was jive. The pay was…

ways. At any event, there was discontent over silly things that were going on. So I decided, in order to rebel, that there was one song that we would always play, and it would end on one big chord. I had to play a D-natural. I just remember that one note that I would always hit. Every night it got a little louder and a little louder and a little longer. Finally we did [?] somewhere, and we hit that chord, and I just hung it over. Ray looks back, and he’s like, “It’s too loud, too loud, damn it, this right here.”…
